beats.narration_text: Ciao — I'm Vedanshu Daxesh Patel. A help-desk bot just told someone they get ten sick days. The real number is fifteen — the policy changed eight months ago. Let's build the broken version, watch it fail, then fix it live with retrieval.

props.command: Show me why a help-desk assistant just gave a wrong answer about sick days — build the broken version, then fix it live.

beats.role_note: the problem, the context, the stakes — BEFORE the CLI loop; no prompt yet
beats.narration_text: Here's the trap: a language model only knows what it saw during training, frozen at some cutoff. Ask it about a policy that changed AFTER that cutoff, and it won't tell you it's guessing — it answers just as fluently as if it were right. The fix isn't a smarter model. It's showing the model the current document before it answers.

show.event: Headline types in: 'Frozen training data can't see today's policy.'
Subline resolves: 'the fix isn't a smarter model — it's the current document, shown before the answer'
Spark line settles: 'Frozen ≠ current'

beats.role_note: ClaudeCodeBeat — the ACTUAL generated code (code/naive_answer.py), trimmed to what teaches
beats.narration_text: Read it before trusting it. TRAINING_SNAPSHOT is the model's entire memory — ten sick days, whatever that was when this thing was trained. Ask it anything about sick days and it can only ever return that one hard-coded number. There's no step in here that looks anything up.

beats.narration_text: That's a bug, not a law of language models. Check the output, then fix the cause: update the script to retrieve the current policy passage from a document store before it answers.

props.segment: Watch Retrieval Fix A Stale Answer.
props.command: claude "that's wrong — the policy changed. Update the script: add a retrieve() step that pulls the CURRENT policy passage from a document store, then answer using that passage."

beats.role_note: ClaudeCodeBeat — the ACTUAL revised code (code/rag_answer.py), trimmed to the diff that matters
beats.narration_text: The diff that matters: one new function, retrieve, that searches the document store for the sick-leave policy and returns the actual passage. Answer no longer invents from memory — it's conditioned on whatever retrieve just found. Same shape as the chapter's own definition: two jobs, wired together.

show.event: Code card rises; retrieve() function highlighted — new since B03
answer() reveals — now conditioned on the retrieved passage

beats.narration_text: Re-run. Fifteen sick days — and this time the answer comes with its receipt: the exact passage it used, updated eight months ago. Nothing about the model changed. Only whether it was handed the current document first.

show.event: '$ python rag_answer.py' title lands
Q: line reveals
Retrieved: line reveals — the full policy passage
A: line reveals — grounded in the retrieved passage
Verdict stamps in terracotta: '✓ grounded, current, cited'

props.title: python rag_answer.py
lines: Q: How many sick days do I get this year?
Retrieved: Effective this year, employees receive 15 sick days annually (updated 8 months ago, replacing the previous 10-day allowance).
A: Based on the current policy: Effective this year, employees receive 15 sick days annually (updated 8 months ago, replacing the previous 10-day allowance).

beats.narration_text: Same toy model, both times — nothing about its reasoning changed. The only difference was whether it was handed the current document before it answered. That's the whole mechanism this chapter names Retrieval-Augmented Generation: retrieve first, generate second, and the second step inherits whatever the first step found.

show.event: Headline types in: 'Same model. Different input.'
Subline resolves: 'retrieval didn't make it smarter — it made the current document part of the question'
Spark line settles: 'Retrieve, then generate.'

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — suggested prompt typed in, viewer-addressed, read-and-discuss
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: 'Take my naive_answer.py-style script — one that only knows a hardcoded fact — and add a retrieve() step that pulls the real, current version of that fact from a small document store I give you. Show me the diff, then run both versions so I can see the wrong answer and the fixed one side by side.' Bring your own stale fact — a policy, a price, a schedule — and check whether the fixed version tells you WHICH passage it used.
